stem: A process is described as performing at a six sigma level. What does this tell you?
options: Its output falls within specification about 99.9% of the time
Its customer limits sit six standard deviations from the process average, about 3.4 defects per million opportunities
It has passed six DMAIC tollgate reviews
It has six process steps between input and output
explanation: Sigma is the symbol for standard deviation. A six sigma process has six standard deviations between its average and the nearest customer limit, which corresponds to about 3.4 defects per million opportunities. It describes performance, not structure (Day 1).
distractor_notes: 99.9% within specification is roughly 4.6 sigma on the table; six sigma is 99.99966%.
DMAIC has five phases and five tollgates, not six.
The number six refers to standard deviations, not process steps.

subtopic: The Problem Solving Strategy Y = f(x)
stem: In the expression Y = f(x), what does Y represent?
options: The financial benefit of the project
The root cause the team must remove
The number of factors in the process
The output or result the project is trying to improve
explanation: Y is the output measure, the result you care about, such as late deliveries per month. The x's are the inputs and process factors that cause it. The strategy is to improve Y by finding and changing the right x's (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Financial benefit may follow from improving Y but is not what Y stands for.
Causes are the x's, not Y.
Y is a single result measure, not a count of factors.

subtopic: Deliverables of a Lean Six Sigma Project
stem: A team has just completed a data collection plan, checked that its measurement system is reliable and established the current defect rate. Which DMAIC phase has it finished?
options: Measure
Define
Improve
Analyse
explanation: Data collection plan, verified measurement system and baseline performance are the deliverables of Measure. Define produces the charter; Analyse produces confirmed causes; Improve produces a piloted solution (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Define ends with a charter and customer requirements, before data is collected.
Improve trials solutions, well after the baseline is set.
Analyse tests causes; it starts once a baseline exists.

stem: Which role selects the project, removes organisational obstacles and approves each tollgate, but does not perform the analysis?
options: Black Belt
Green Belt
Champion
Master Black Belt
explanation: The Champion, also called the sponsor, is the senior manager who owns the business problem. They choose the project, clear obstacles and sign off tollgates. Analysis is done by the Green or Black Belt leading the project (Day 1).
distractor_notes: A Black Belt leads complex projects full-time and does the analysis.
A Green Belt leads smaller projects and does the analysis part-time.
A Master Black Belt coaches belts and runs the programme; they are not the project's sponsor.

subtopic: Voice of the Customer, Business and Employee
stem: A project team is deciding how to define a "defective invoice". Which source should the definition come from?
options: The voice of the employee, because staff know which invoices are hard to produce
The Black Belt's judgement, because they have the most training
The voice of the business, because invoices affect cash flow
The voice of the customer, because a defect is a failure to meet a customer requirement
explanation: A defect is any output that fails a customer requirement, so the definition of a defective invoice must come from what the customer needs. The business and employee voices matter for why the project is funded and where causes lie, but not for defining defects (Day 1).
distractor_notes: The voice of the employee helps find causes, not define requirements.
Requirements come from customers, not from the belt's opinion.
The voice of the business explains why the project matters, not what counts as a defect.

subtopic: General History of Six Sigma & Continuous Improvement
stem: Where did Six Sigma originate?
options: Toyota, Japan, in the 1950s
Motorola, United States, in the 1980s
Ford, United States, in the 1910s
General Electric, United States, in the 1990s
explanation: Six Sigma was developed at Motorola in the 1980s, with engineer Bill Smith usually credited. General Electric adopted and popularised it in the 1990s. Toyota is the origin of Lean, not Six Sigma (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Toyota is where Lean came from.
Ford's assembly line influenced Lean thinking but is not the origin of Six Sigma.
GE made Six Sigma famous but did not invent it.

subtopic: General History of Six Sigma & Continuous Improvement
stem: Lean thinking developed mainly from which source?
options: The Toyota Production System
Motorola's quality programme
The United States military's sampling standards
Bell Laboratories' control chart work
explanation: Lean grew out of the Toyota Production System, developed in Japan after the Second World War by engineers including Taiichi Ohno. It focuses on removing waste so value flows faster (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Motorola is the origin of Six Sigma.
Military sampling standards contributed to acceptance sampling, not Lean.
Bell Labs (Walter Shewhart) gave us control charts, which are a Six Sigma tool.

stem: Which statement best distinguishes the focus of Lean from the focus of Six Sigma?
options: Lean applies to manufacturing; Six Sigma applies to services
Lean removes waste and delay; Six Sigma reduces variation and defects
Lean reduces variation; Six Sigma removes waste
Lean uses statistics; Six Sigma uses visual management
explanation: Lean asks which steps add value and removes the rest, attacking waste and delay. Six Sigma asks how much output varies from requirements and finds the causes of that variation. Both apply to any industry (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Both methods apply to manufacturing and services alike.
This reverses the two.
Statistics belong mainly to Six Sigma; visual management is a Lean tool.

subtopic: Deliverables of a Lean Six Sigma Project
stem: Which deliverable belongs to the Control phase?
options: Control plan and monitoring chart handed to the process owner
Baseline defect rate
List of confirmed root causes
Project charter
explanation: Control makes sure the improvement lasts: a control plan, monitoring charts and updated procedures are handed to the process owner. The charter is Define, the baseline is Measure and confirmed causes are Analyse (Day 1).
distractor_notes: The baseline is produced in Measure.
Confirmed causes are the output of Analyse.
The charter is produced in Define.

subtopic: Deliverables of a Lean Six Sigma Project
stem: What is the purpose of a tollgate review?
options: To let the team choose which DMAIC phase to do next
To have the sponsor confirm a phase's deliverables are complete before the next phase starts
To train Yellow Belts in the tools used so far
To measure the process capability at the end of the project
explanation: A tollgate is the review at the end of each phase where the Champion checks the deliverables and approves moving on. DMAIC phases run in a fixed order, so the review is about readiness, not choosing a direction (Day 1).
distractor_notes: The phase order is fixed: Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control.
Training is not the purpose of a tollgate.
Capability is measured in Measure and rechecked in Control, not at tollgates as such.

subtopic: The Problem Solving Strategy Y = f(x)
stem: A call centre wants to cut average call handling time. A team member proposes "measure handling time every day and display it on a big screen so people try harder." In terms of Y = f(x), what is the weakness of this proposal?
options: It confuses the voice of the customer with the voice of the business
It uses too many x's at once
It measures the wrong Y; call volume should be measured instead
It acts only on Y and does not identify or change any x that causes long calls
explanation: Handling time is the Y. Displaying Y more prominently does not change the causes of long calls, such as system lookups, unclear scripts or call transfers. Y = f(x) says you change results by changing the x's that drive them (Day 1).
distractor_notes: The proposal is not about which voice is used.
The proposal names no x's at all.
Handling time is a reasonable Y for this problem.

stem: Which description best fits a Green Belt?
options: Trains Black Belts and manages the organisation's improvement programme
Owns the business problem and funds the project
Leads smaller projects in their own area, usually part-time alongside a normal job
Works full-time on improvement and leads complex cross-functional projects
explanation: Green Belts keep their normal role and lead smaller, local projects part-time. Black Belts are full-time on complex projects, Master Black Belts coach and run the programme, and the Champion owns and funds the problem (Day 1).
distractor_notes: That describes a Master Black Belt.
That describes the Champion or sponsor.
That describes a Black Belt.

stem: At the end of the Control phase, who takes responsibility for keeping the improved process running day to day?
options: The Master Black Belt
The Champion
The Green Belt who led the project
The process owner
explanation: The process owner is the manager responsible for the process in normal operation. Control ends with handover to them, including the control plan and monitoring charts. The belt moves on to the next project (Day 1).
distractor_notes: The Master Black Belt coaches belts; they do not run processes.
The Champion sponsors projects; the process owner runs the process.
The Green Belt hands the process back and moves to other work.

subtopic: Voice of the Customer, Business and Employee
stem: "Each late shipment costs us about $9 in refunds, which is roughly $13 000 a month." Which voice is this statement an example of?
options: Voice of the business
Voice of the customer
Voice of the employee
Voice of the process
explanation: Cost, margin and financial impact are the voice of the business: they explain why the organisation should fund the project. The customer's voice would describe what "late" means to them; the employee's voice would describe obstacles in doing the work (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Customers care about receiving parcels on time, not about the company's refund costs.
Employees' voice is about how the work feels and where it goes wrong.
"Voice of the process" describes measured process behaviour, not money.

subtopic: Voice of the Customer, Business and Employee
stem: Which of these is the most direct method of collecting the voice of the customer?
options: Reviewing the annual budget
Interviewing customers and analysing their complaints
Reading the team's shift handover notes
Calculating the process sigma level
explanation: The voice of the customer is gathered from customers themselves: interviews, surveys, complaints and observation. Budgets are the voice of the business, handover notes the voice of the employee, and sigma level is a process measure (Day 1).
distractor_notes: The budget reflects the business's needs, not the customer's.
Handover notes capture the employee's view.
Sigma level is a measurement of the process, not a customer input.

stem: Which statement about the term "sigma" is correct?
options: Sigma is the Greek letter used for standard deviation, a measure of spread
Sigma is the number of steps in a process
Sigma is the number of defects found per unit
Sigma is the Greek letter used for the mean of a population
explanation: Sigma (σ) is the statistical symbol for standard deviation, which measures how spread out values are. The mean is written μ (mu). Defects per unit and step counts have their own names (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Step count is not a statistical symbol.
Defects per unit is DPU.
The population mean is μ, not σ.

subtopic: Deliverables of a Lean Six Sigma Project
stem: A team ran a two-week trial of a new sorting screen on one shift and showed the late-parcel rate fell from 12% to 7% on that shift. Which phase does this work belong to, and what should come next?
options: Improve; next, roll the change out fully and move to Control with a control plan and handover
Control; next, pilot the solution on other shifts
Measure; next, brainstorm causes
Analyse; next, write the project charter
explanation: Piloting a solution and showing it moves Y is the Improve phase. The next phase is Control: standardise the change, set up monitoring and hand over so the gain holds. Charters come first (Define) and cause-finding is Analyse (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Piloting belongs to Improve; Control comes after the pilot succeeds.
Measure establishes the baseline before causes are tested.
Analyse finds causes; the charter was written back in Define.

subtopic: General History of Six Sigma & Continuous Improvement
stem: Why were Lean and Six Sigma combined into a single method?
options: Because Six Sigma had been discredited and needed a new name
Because a process can be fast but error-prone, or accurate but slow, and the two methods address these different problems
Because regulators required both
Because Lean only works in Japan and Six Sigma only works in the United States
explanation: Lean attacks delay and waste; Six Sigma attacks variation and defects. A process usually needs both. Combining them lets one project use whichever tools the problem calls for (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Six Sigma was not discredited; it remains widely used.
No regulator requires either method.
Both methods are used worldwide across industries.

subtopic: The Problem Solving Strategy Y = f(x)
stem: In Y = f(x), which of the following is an example of an x rather than a Y?
options: Average minutes to resolve a ticket
Which supplier provided the packaging
Percentage of orders shipped late
Number of complaints per month
explanation: The supplier used is an input factor that may cause a result, so it is an x. The other three are all output measures (results) and would be Y's (Day 1).
distractor_notes: Resolution time is a result: a Y.
Late shipment percentage is a result, so it is a Y.
Complaints per month is a result: a Y.

stem: Which role provides basic awareness-level support, such as helping to collect data during a project?
options: Champion
Master Black Belt
Black Belt
Yellow Belt
explanation: Yellow Belts (and White Belts in some schemes) have basic training and support projects as team members, often collecting data or joining improvement events. The other roles lead, coach or sponsor (Day 1).
distractor_notes: The Champion sponsors the project.
The Master Black Belt coaches belts and runs the programme.
Black Belts lead complex projects full-time.

stem: A claims clerk walks to a shared printer about 40 times a day to collect printed forms. Which of the seven wastes does the walking represent?
options: Motion
Over-processing
Waiting
Transport
explanation: Motion is movement of people that adds no value: walking, reaching, searching. The clerk is moving, not the forms. Transport would be the forms themselves being carried between locations (Day 2).
distractor_notes: Over-processing is doing more work per item than needed, such as extra approvals.
Waiting is idle time; the clerk is busy, not idle.
Transport is movement of the item being worked on, not of the person.

stem: Which list gives the five Lean principles in the order described by Womack and Jones?
options: Value, value stream, flow, pull, perfection
Flow, pull, value, value stream, perfection
Value stream, value, pull, flow, perfection
Perfection, value, flow, pull, value stream
explanation: The principles run from defining what the customer values, through mapping the value stream, making it flow, letting the customer pull, and then repeating the cycle in pursuit of perfection (Day 2).
distractor_notes: Value must be specified before anything else.
Value comes before the value stream, and flow comes before pull.
Perfection is the last principle, not the first.

stem: In an insurance claims process, which of the following activities is value-added according to the three-part Lean test?
options: The claim file waits in a queue for the assessor to become free
The assessor calculates the payout from the policy terms and the damage report
The claim is photocopied for a backup paper file
A second manager re-checks the claim amount that the first manager already approved
explanation: Calculating the payout transforms the claim towards its outcome, the customer would pay for it and, done correctly, it is done once. The other options are over-processing, waiting and over-processing again: none changes the claim in a way the customer values (Day 2).
distractor_notes: Queue time is waiting, a non-value-added activity.
A backup copy does not change the claim or move it forward.
A repeated check adds no transformation; it is over-processing.

stem: What are the two pillars of the Toyota Production System?
options: Kaizen and 5S
Push production and batch processing
Just-in-time and jidoka
Six Sigma and statistical process control
explanation: The Toyota Production System rests on just-in-time (make only what is needed, when needed) and jidoka (stop the process when a defect appears and fix it at the source). Kaizen and 5S are practices within it, not the pillars (Day 2).
distractor_notes: Kaizen and 5S are Lean practices but are not named as the two pillars.
Push and batching are what the Toyota Production System replaced.
Six Sigma and statistical process control come from Motorola and Bell Labs, not Toyota.

stem: Which publication popularised the word "Lean" as the name for Toyota's production approach?
options: Motorola's Six Sigma training material of the 1980s
Taiichi Ohno's internal Toyota manuals of the 1950s
The 1990 MIT study published as The Machine That Changed the World
Henry Ford's 1913 description of the moving assembly line
explanation: The term "lean production" was coined by researcher John Krafcik in 1988 and popularised by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology study published in 1990 as The Machine That Changed the World, by Womack, Jones and Roos. Toyota called its approach the Toyota Production System (Day 2).
distractor_notes: Motorola's material is the origin of Six Sigma, not the word Lean.
Ohno developed the system but the English word Lean came later, from the MIT study.
Ford's line was an early example of flow but the term Lean did not exist then.

stem: A loan approval process takes 15 working days, of which about 14 are spent waiting between steps. Applications are almost never approved incorrectly. Which set of tools should the Green Belt reach for first?
options: A larger inspection team to check each application
Hypothesis tests and capability analysis to find the sources of variation
Value stream mapping, batch-size reduction and pull to remove waiting
A new customer survey to redefine the requirement
explanation: The problem is delay, not defects, so it is a Lean problem. Value stream mapping shows where the waiting sits, and smaller batches and pull remove it. Six Sigma's statistical tools are for variation and defects, which this process does not have (Day 2).
distractor_notes: More inspection adds appraisal cost and does nothing about waiting.
Statistical tools attack variation and defects; the process has a delay problem.
The requirement (approve quickly and correctly) is not in doubt.

stem: In 5S, giving every remaining item a fixed, labelled location close to where it is used belongs to which step?
options: Sort
Shine
Straighten
Standardise
explanation: Straighten (also called Set in Order) is "a place for everything and everything in its place": shadow boards, labels and marked floor areas. Sort removes what is not needed, Shine cleans, and Standardise writes the arrangement down (Day 2).
distractor_notes: Sort is removing unneeded items, which happens before locations are assigned.
Shine is cleaning and inspecting.
Standardise documents the agreed arrangement so everyone keeps it the same.

stem: Why did Taiichi Ohno describe overproduction as the worst of the seven wastes?
options: Because it only occurs in manufacturing
Because it is the hardest waste to measure
Because it is the only waste that customers notice
Because it generates the other wastes: inventory, transport, motion, waiting and hidden defects
explanation: Making too much or too early creates inventory, which must be moved and stored, causes people to walk around it, sits waiting, and hides defects until the items are finally used. Overproduction manufactures the other wastes (Day 2).
distractor_notes: Overproduction occurs in offices too, such as printing reports nobody reads.
Overproduction is easy to measure: count what was made against what was needed.
Customers notice defects and waiting more directly than overproduction.

stem: A signed contract is couriered from the Sydney office to the Perth office for a second signature and then couriered back. Which waste is this an example of?
options: Overproduction
Motion
Inventory
Transport
explanation: The item being worked on, the contract, is being moved between locations. That is transport. Motion would be the person walking or searching; here the people stay put and the document travels (Day 2).
distractor_notes: Nothing extra is being produced.
Motion is movement of people; here it is the document that moves.
Inventory is items held and not being worked on; the contract is in transit, not stockpiled.

stem: Which statement correctly describes a pull system?
options: Work is inspected at every step before it is passed on
Work is started only when the next step, and ultimately the customer, signals a need for it
Work is grouped into large batches to reduce the number of changeovers
Work is released according to a forecast so that machines are never idle
explanation: Pull means producing to actual demand: the downstream step or the customer triggers the work. Producing to a forecast or schedule regardless of demand is push, which builds inventory between steps (Day 2).
distractor_notes: Inspection at each step describes appraisal, not the pull principle.
Large batches are the opposite of flow and are not what defines pull.
Producing to a forecast is push, not pull.

stem: A regulator requires that every export shipment is checked against a sanctions list before it leaves. How does Lean classify this check?
options: Waste, to be eliminated at the first opportunity
Value-added, because it is legally required
Overproduction, because it produces a record nobody reads
Business non-value-added: necessary, but to be made as small as possible
explanation: The check does not transform the shipment and the customer would not choose to pay for it, so it is not value-added. Because it is required, Lean calls it business non-value-added (or necessary non-value-added) and works to make it quick and cheap rather than remove it (Day 2).
distractor_notes: The check cannot be removed while the law requires it.
Legal necessity does not make an activity value-added; it still fails the transformation test.
The check is not making excess output.

stem: Ten forms are processed as a batch through three steps. Each step takes one minute per form, and a step does not start until the whole batch arrives. At what minute is the first form completely finished?
options: 21 minutes
3 minutes
12 minutes
30 minutes
explanation: Step 1 finishes the batch at minute 10 and step 2 at minute 20. Step 3 then completes the first form at minute 21. In one-piece flow the first form would be finished at minute 3, which shows what batching costs (Day 2).
distractor_notes: 3 minutes is the one-piece-flow result, not the batch result.
12 minutes is when the last form is finished under one-piece flow.
30 minutes is when the last form is finished, not the first.

stem: A supervisor audits the workshop every week against the agreed 5S standard and coaches staff who let it slip. Which 5S step is this?
options: Standardise
Shine
Self-discipline
Sort
explanation: Self-discipline (also called Sustain) is making the standard a habit through audits, training and management attention. Standardise is the earlier step of writing the standard down; auditing against it is Self-discipline (Day 2).
distractor_notes: Standardise creates the written standard and photographs; auditing against them is the next step.
Shine is cleaning and inspection.
Sort removes unneeded items.

stem: What does jidoka mean in the Toyota Production System?
options: Producing only what is needed, when it is needed
Organising the workplace in five steps
Continuous small improvements by the people who do the work
Stopping the process as soon as a defect is detected so the problem is fixed at its source
explanation: Jidoka, sometimes translated as "automation with a human touch", gives machines and people the ability to stop the line when something goes wrong so that defects are not passed on. It builds quality in rather than inspecting it in (Day 2).
distractor_notes: Producing only what is needed is just-in-time, the other pillar.
The five-step workplace method is 5S.
Continuous small improvements are kaizen.

stem: A shared mailbox holds 1 200 customer requests that nobody has opened yet. Which of the seven wastes best describes this?
options: Transport
Motion
Over-processing
Inventory
explanation: Inventory is anything held that is not being worked on right now, and that includes information. Unopened requests are work in process sitting in a queue, exactly like pallets beside a machine (Day 2).
distractor_notes: The requests are not being moved between locations.
Nobody is moving; the requests are sitting still.
No work at all is being done on the requests, so it cannot be excess work.

stem: A team used value stream mapping and smaller batches to cut a lab's turnaround time from 12 hours to 4 hours, but the rate of mislabelled samples stayed at 8%. What should the team do next?
options: Reduce batch size further, because Lean tools solve all process problems
Declare the project complete because lead time was the primary metric
Use Six Sigma tools to collect data on the mislabelling and find its causes
Add a full-time checker to catch mislabelled samples
explanation: Delay was a Lean problem and Lean fixed it. Defects are a variation problem, which is what Six Sigma's data-driven cause-finding is for. That is why the two are combined: each addresses what the other leaves behind (Day 2).
distractor_notes: Batch size affects waiting, not why labels are wrong.
An 8% defect rate is a live problem whether or not it was the primary metric, and the team was asked what to do next.
A checker is appraisal cost that catches defects instead of preventing them.

stem: What is kaizen?
options: A method for calculating the sigma level of a process
The Japanese name for the Six Sigma belt system
Continuous small improvements made by the people who do the work
A one-off large investment in new equipment
explanation: Kaizen means improvement in small steps, made continuously and mostly by the workers themselves, often in short focused events. It is part of the Toyota Production System and of the continuous improvement habit (Day 2).
distractor_notes: Sigma level is a Six Sigma metric unrelated to kaizen.
Belts are a Six Sigma idea from Motorola and GE, not a Japanese term.
Kaizen is the opposite of a one-off large investment.

stem: During the Sort step of 5S, what is a red tag used for?
options: To mark items whose need is uncertain so they can be removed if nobody claims them within an agreed period
To mark items that have been cleaned and inspected
To mark the standard location of a tool on a shadow board
To mark the results of the weekly audit
explanation: Sort removes everything not needed for the current work. Items nobody is sure about get a red tag and go to a holding area; if nobody claims them in the agreed time they are removed. The other options describe Shine, Straighten and Self-discipline (Day 2).
distractor_notes: Cleaning and inspection is Shine, which does not use red tags.
Locations and shadow boards belong to Straighten.
Audits belong to Self-discipline.

stem: Which of the following is a Lean tool rather than a Six Sigma tool?
options: 5S
Process capability index
Control chart
Hypothesis test
explanation: 5S organises the workplace to remove waste, which is Lean's purpose. Hypothesis tests, capability indices and control charts are statistical tools used to understand and reduce variation, which is Six Sigma's purpose (Day 2).
distractor_notes: Capability indices measure variation against specifications, a Six Sigma tool.
Control charts come from Shewhart's statistical work and belong to Six Sigma.
Hypothesis tests are Six Sigma statistics.

stem: A sample spends 101.6 minutes in a laboratory process from collection to result. Only the centrifuge (10 minutes) and the analyser (12 minutes) transform the sample. What percentage of the time is value-added?
explanation: Value-added time is 10 + 12 = 22 minutes. 22 ÷ 101.6 = 0.217, or 21.7%. The remaining 78.3% is waiting, transport, motion, over-processing and rework (Day 2).
distractor_notes: 78.3% is the non-value-added share, the complement of the answer.
45.5% divides 10 by 22, comparing the two value-added steps with each other.
9.8% uses only the centrifuge time (10 ÷ 101.6).

subtopic: Basic Six Sigma Metrics (DPU, DPMO, FTY, RTY, Cycle Time)
stem: An audit of 500 invoices found 60 defects spread over 45 invoices. What is the DPU (defects per unit)?
explanation: DPU is total defects divided by total units: 60 ÷ 500 = 0.12. The 45 defective invoices are not used for DPU; they would be used for yield (Day 3).
distractor_notes: 8.33 is 500 ÷ 60, the division the wrong way round.
0.024 is DPO, which divides by opportunities as well.
0.09 is 45 ÷ 500, the proportion of defective units, not defects per unit.

subtopic: Basic Six Sigma Metrics (DPU, DPMO, FTY, RTY, Cycle Time)
stem: A purchase order has 6 fields that can be wrong. In 400 orders, 48 defects were found. What is the DPO (defects per opportunity)?
explanation: Total opportunities are 400 × 6 = 2 400. DPO = 48 ÷ 2 400 = 0.02. Dividing by units alone would give DPU (Day 3).
distractor_notes: 0.12 is DPU (48 ÷ 400); DPO also divides by opportunities per unit.
0.0033 divides 48 by 400 × 6 × 6, applying the opportunity count twice.
0.08 is 48 ÷ 600, using opportunities plus units instead of their product.

subtopic: Basic Six Sigma Metrics (DPU, DPMO, FTY, RTY, Cycle Time)
stem: A packing line inspects 700 cartons, each with 4 opportunities for a defect, and finds 35 defects. What is the DPMO?
distractor_notes: 200,000 is 35 ÷ 700 × 4 × 1 000 000, multiplying by opportunities instead of dividing.
50,000 is DPU × 1 000 000 (35 ÷ 700), forgetting the opportunities.
3,125 divides by 700 × 4 × 4.

subtopic: Basic Six Sigma Metrics (DPU, DPMO, FTY, RTY, Cycle Time)
stem: An inspector finds three errors on one insurance application form. How is this recorded in Six Sigma terms?
options: One defective and three defects
One defective and one defect
Three defectives and one defect
Three defectives and three defects
explanation: A defect is one failure to meet a requirement; a defective is a unit with at least one defect. One form with three errors is one defective unit carrying three defects. DPU uses the defect count; yield uses the defective count (Day 3).
distractor_notes: Each error is a separate defect, so there are three.
The counts are the wrong way round.
There is only one unit, so there can be only one defective.

subtopic: Basic Six Sigma Metrics (DPU, DPMO, FTY, RTY, Cycle Time)
stem: A four-step process has first time yields of 96%, 97%, 95% and 98%. What is the rolled throughput yield?
explanation: Rolled throughput yield multiplies the step yields: 0.96 × 0.97 × 0.95 × 0.98 = 0.8669, about 86.7%. Only 87 units in 100 pass every step untouched (Day 3).
distractor_notes: 98.0% is the best single step.
95.0% is the worst single step, not the combined yield.
96.5% is the average of the four yields; RTY multiplies, it does not average.

subtopic: Basic Six Sigma Metrics (DPU, DPMO, FTY, RTY, Cycle Time)
stem: 1,200 pumps entered final test. 1,080 passed without any rework. A further 60 failed, were repaired and then passed; 60 were scrapped. What is the first time yield of the test step?
explanation: First time yield counts only units that passed without rework: 1 080 ÷ 1 200 = 0.90, or 90%. The 60 repaired pumps did eventually pass, but not the first time, so they are excluded (Day 3).
distractor_notes: 95.0% includes the repaired pumps (1 140 ÷ 1 200); that is final yield, which hides rework.
85.0% subtracts both the repaired and the scrapped pumps twice over.
5.0% is the scrap rate, not a yield.

subtopic: Basic Six Sigma Metrics (DPU, DPMO, FTY, RTY, Cycle Time)
stem: A process runs at 24,000 DPMO. Using the standard sigma table (which includes the 1.5-sigma shift), what is its sigma level, to two decimal places?
explanation: 24 000 DPMO is a defect proportion of 0.024, so 97.6% of opportunities are defect-free. On the normal distribution that is 1.98 standard deviations; the standard table adds the 1.5 shift to give 3.48 sigma (Day 3).
distractor_notes: 2.50 is a guess halfway between 2 and 3 sigma; the table value is 3.48.
1.98 is the long-term value without the 1.5 shift; the standard table includes the shift.
4.98 adds the 1.5 shift twice.

stem: A customer returns a faulty appliance under warranty and the company pays for the repair and the freight. Into which cost of poor quality category does this fall?
options: Prevention cost
External failure cost
Internal failure cost
Appraisal cost
explanation: The defect was found after delivery to the customer, so the repair, freight and claim handling are external failure costs, the most expensive category per defect (Day 3).
distractor_notes: Prevention is the cost of stopping defects before they happen.
Internal failure is for defects caught before the customer receives the product.
Appraisal is the cost of inspecting and testing.

stem: A pharmaceutical plant employs four analysts to test every batch before release. Most batches pass. How is the analysts' cost classified?
options: Appraisal cost, because it is the cost of checking for defects
Internal failure cost, because it is triggered by the possibility of defects
External failure cost, because it protects the customer
Prevention cost, because testing stops bad batches reaching patients
explanation: Testing and inspection are appraisal costs whether or not they find anything. Prevention would be work that stops defects being made in the first place, such as process design or training. Failure costs are incurred only when defects actually occur (Day 3).
distractor_notes: Internal failure costs arise from actual defects (scrap, rework), not from checking.
External failure is incurred after the customer has received a defect.
Testing finds defects; it does not prevent them from being made.

stem:
A hospital pharmacy classified 240 dispensing errors from the last quarter:

| Error type | Count |
|---|---|
| Wrong dose | 96 |
| Wrong patient label | 72 |
| Wrong drug | 30 |
| Missing instructions | 24 |
| Late dispensing | 18 |

Using Pareto analysis, which error types are the vital few the project should address first?
options: Wrong drug and late dispensing, because they are the most dangerous
All five types equally, because each is a patient safety risk
Wrong dose and wrong patient label, which together account for 70% of the errors
Missing instructions, because it is the easiest to fix
explanation: Sorted from largest to smallest, wrong dose (96) and wrong patient label (72) total 168 of 240 errors, or 70%. Two of five categories produce most of the effect: those are the vital few. Pareto by count says start there (Day 3).
distractor_notes: Pareto by count ranks by frequency. Danger might justify a separate Pareto by severity, but the question asks for count-based analysis.
Treating every category equally is what Pareto analysis exists to avoid.
Ease of fixing is not a Pareto criterion.

stem: What does the 80:20 rule state?
options: Exactly 80% of defects always come from exactly 20% of defect types
Roughly 80% of an effect comes from roughly 20% of the causes
80% of projects fail and 20% succeed
A process should be at least 80% efficient and no more than 20% waste
explanation: The Pareto principle, named after Vilfredo Pareto and applied to quality by Joseph Juran, observes that a small number of causes (the vital few) produce most of the effect. The split is rarely exactly 80:20 (Day 3).
distractor_notes: The split is approximate; 70:30 or 90:10 are equally consistent with the principle.
The rule is about causes and effects, not project success rates.
The rule says nothing about efficiency targets.

stem: Sixty invoice defects were classified: purchase order number 27, line items 18, address 8, total 4, customer name 3. What is the cumulative percentage after the two largest categories on a Pareto chart?
explanation: Sort largest first: 27 then 18. Cumulative count after two categories is 45. 45 ÷ 60 × 100 = 75.0%. The cumulative line on the chart passes through 45.0% after the first bar and 75.0% after the second (Day 3).
distractor_notes: 30.0% is the second category on its own.
88.3% is the cumulative percentage after three categories.
45.0% is the cumulative percentage after only the first category.

subtopic: Basic Six Sigma Metrics (DPU, DPMO, FTY, RTY, Cycle Time)
stem: Two suppliers both deliver in an average of 5.0 days. Supplier A's deliveries range from 4.5 to 5.5 days; Supplier B's range from 2 to 8 days. The customer needs delivery within 6 days. Which statement is correct?
options: Neither supplier meets the need, because 5.0 days is too close to 6
The suppliers perform equally because their averages are the same
Supplier B is better because some deliveries arrive in 2 days
Supplier A is better because its smaller variation means every delivery meets the 6-day need
explanation: Customers experience individual deliveries, not averages. Supplier A's spread stays inside the requirement every time; Supplier B's spread produces late deliveries even though its average is identical. Variation, not the average, is what creates defects (Day 3).
distractor_notes: An average of 5.0 with a spread of 4.5 to 5.5 meets a 6-day limit comfortably.
Equal averages hide very different spreads; the spread decides how many defects occur.
Early deliveries do not compensate the customers who receive 8-day deliveries.

subtopic: Basic Six Sigma Metrics (DPU, DPMO, FTY, RTY, Cycle Time)
stem: What is the difference between cycle time and lead time?
options: They are two names for the same measure
Cycle time is the time to complete one unit once work starts; lead time is the total time from customer request to delivery, including waiting
Lead time applies only to manufacturing; cycle time applies only to services
Cycle time is measured in days; lead time is measured in hours
explanation: Cycle time is what the process is doing to a unit; lead time is what the customer waits, which includes every queue and delay. Lead time is usually much longer than cycle time because of waiting. Some Lean texts also use cycle time for the interval between successive units leaving a process; the exam contrast is always cycle time versus lead time (Day 3).
distractor_notes: They differ by the waiting time between and before steps.
Both terms apply to any process.
Both can be measured in any time unit.

stem: What is meant by the "hidden factory"?
options: The spare capacity a plant keeps for demand peaks
The scrap and warranty costs that appear in the monthly accounts
The rework, checking and workarounds that exist only to fix the output of the official process and rarely appear in the accounts
The prevention activities that a company does not publicise
explanation: The hidden factory is the unofficial second process, often large, that reworks and re-checks defective output. Its cost is mostly invisible in normal reporting, which is why cost of poor quality is usually far larger than the visible scrap and warranty figures (Day 3).
distractor_notes: Spare capacity is a planning decision, not the hidden factory.
Scrap and warranty are the visible part of the cost of poor quality, the opposite of hidden.
Prevention is a deliberate, visible category of quality cost.

subtopic: Basic Six Sigma Metrics (DPU, DPMO, FTY, RTY, Cycle Time)
stem: Why does the standard sigma table equate 3.4 defects per million opportunities with six sigma, when the normal distribution places six standard deviations at about 0.002 defects per million?
options: Because defects per million opportunities and defects per million units are different measures
Because the table was calculated before computers
Because the table builds in a 1.5-sigma shift to allow for long-term drift of the process mean, so 6 sigma short-term is treated as 4.5 sigma long-term
Because the table rounds heavily
explanation: Motorola's convention is that a process measured over a short period drifts by about 1.5 standard deviations over the long run. The table adds 1.5 to the value the normal distribution gives, so 4.5 sigma on the normal curve (3.4 DPMO) is reported as 6 sigma (Day 3).
distractor_notes: Both figures are per opportunity; the difference is the shift.
The table is exact given the shift convention.
Rounding does not account for a difference of three orders of magnitude.

stem: A company spends $30,000 training operators in a new set-up procedure and installing fixtures that make wrong assembly impossible. Which cost of poor quality category is this?
options: Internal failure cost
Appraisal cost
Prevention cost
External failure cost
explanation: Training and mistake-proofing stop defects being made in the first place, which is prevention. Appraisal would be inspecting the assemblies afterwards; failure costs arise only when defects actually occur (Day 3).
distractor_notes: Internal failure is scrap and rework of actual defects.
Appraisal is inspection and testing, not training or fixtures.
External failure is defects reaching the customer.

stem: A Pareto chart of complaint counts shows "late delivery" as the tallest bar (48% of complaints) and "damaged goods" as a small bar (6%). The finance team points out that a damaged-goods complaint costs about 15 times as much to resolve as a late-delivery complaint. What should the Green Belt do?
options: Build a second Pareto chart weighted by cost and compare the two rankings before choosing
Ignore the cost data, because Pareto charts must use counts
Combine the two categories into one bar
Address damaged goods only, because cost always outranks frequency
explanation: Pareto by count and Pareto by cost can rank categories differently. At 15 times the cost, damaged goods (6% × 15 = 90 units of cost) outweighs late delivery (48 units) on a cost basis. The right move is to draw both and choose with the Champion (Day 3).
distractor_notes: Pareto charts can be built on counts, cost, time or any measure of effect.
Combining unrelated categories destroys the information the chart is meant to give.
Neither count nor cost automatically wins; the decision depends on the project's goal.

subtopic: Basic Six Sigma Metrics (DPU, DPMO, FTY, RTY, Cycle Time)
stem: A team wants its invoice process to look better and proposes counting every character on the invoice as a separate opportunity for a defect. Why is this wrong?
options: Because inflating the opportunity count lowers DPO and DPMO without any real improvement, and opportunities should be limited to distinct features the customer would see as defects
Because opportunities must always equal the number of process steps
Because DPMO can only be calculated with exactly one opportunity per unit
Because characters cannot be counted reliably
explanation: Opportunities are defined in advance as the distinct ways a unit can fail a requirement. Adding opportunities that never fail makes the same 60 defects look like a much smaller proportion. The process has not changed; only the denominator has (Day 3).
distractor_notes: Opportunities are features that can be wrong, not process steps.
DPMO works for any number of opportunities per unit.
Counting is possible; the problem is that the count is padded.

stem: Which of the following is a properly stated critical to quality characteristic (CTQ)?
options: Staff should be well trained
The call centre should try harder
Calls must be answered within 30 seconds, with a target of 15 seconds
Customers want friendly service
explanation: A CTQ is a customer need translated into a measurable characteristic with a target and a limit. "Answered within 30 seconds" can be measured and has a specification; "friendly service" is a need that has not yet been translated (Day 4).
distractor_notes: Training is an input, not a characteristic of the output.
That is an instruction with no measure.
That is a need in the customer's words, not yet measurable.

stem: A CTQ tree for a courier has these levels: "Arrive when you said you would" → "Parcel loaded on the correct van" → "Parcel arrival time relative to the promised window; target inside the window; limit no later than the window closes". What are the three levels, in order?
options: CTQ, driver, need
Need, driver, CTQ
Requirement, specification, target
Voice of the business, voice of the customer, voice of the employee
explanation: A CTQ tree drills from the need in the customer's words, through the drivers that must happen for the need to be met, to the measurable CTQ with its target and limit (Day 4).
distractor_notes: The order is reversed.
Specification and target are parts of the CTQ, not the tree's levels.
The three voices are sources of requirements, not levels of a CTQ tree.

stem: What is the purpose of an operational definition?
options: To describe exactly how a measure is taken so that different people measuring the same thing get the same answer
To list the process steps in a SIPOC
To record the customer's needs in their own words
To state the financial value of a CTQ
explanation: An operational definition removes ambiguity from a measure: what counts, which clock or record is used, and how borderline cases are handled. Without one, data collected in Measure means different things to different people (Day 4).
distractor_notes: Process steps are in the SIPOC, a different tool.
Needs in the customer's words are the top of the CTQ tree.
Financial value is the business case, not the operational definition.

stem: When a team sets out to define a process for a project, what should it agree first?
options: The statistical test to be used
The solution to be piloted
The first step that triggers the process and the last step where the output is handed over
The root cause of the problem
explanation: Defining a process starts with its boundaries: where it begins and where it ends. Inputs, outputs, the owner and the high-level steps follow. Causes, tests and solutions belong to later phases (Day 5).
distractor_notes: Tests are chosen in Analyse.
Solutions belong to Improve.
Root causes are found in Analyse, after the process has been defined and measured.

stem: A project on late customer deliveries defined its process as starting when the parcel is scanned into the local depot. In Analyse the team finds most lateness is caused by parcels arriving late from the interstate hub, which is outside the defined boundary. What does this show?
options: The team should ignore the finding because it is out of scope
The process boundary was set too narrow and the scope should be revisited with the Champion
Analyse was performed incorrectly
The interstate hub should be added to the team without changing the charter
explanation: A boundary chosen too narrow can leave the main cause outside the project. The correct response is to go back to the charter and agree a change of scope with the Champion, not to pretend the cause does not exist or to widen the work informally (Day 4).
distractor_notes: Ignoring the main cause guarantees the project fails to move the Y.
Analyse did its job: it found the cause.
Scope changes are made in the charter with the Champion's agreement, not by quietly adding people.

stem: In the Kano model, which kind of customer need causes strong dissatisfaction when it is missing but earns almost no extra satisfaction when it is met?
options: Delighter
Secondary need
Performance need
Basic (must-be) need
explanation: Basic needs are expected without being asked, such as brakes that work or a bill that adds up. Meeting them is taken for granted; missing them causes anger. Performance needs work in both directions and delighters please when present but are not missed (Day 4).
distractor_notes: Delighters do the opposite: they please when present and are not missed when absent.
Secondary need is not a Kano category.
Performance needs raise satisfaction as they improve and lower it as they worsen.

subtopic: Basic Six Sigma Metrics (DPU, DPMO, FTY, RTY, Cycle Time)
stem: A process runs at 6,210 defects per million opportunities. What is its sigma level on the standard sigma table?
explanation: 6 210 DPMO is the standard-table landmark for 4 sigma (with the 1.5 shift included). The landmarks worth memorising are 3 sigma 66 807, 4 sigma 6 210, 5 sigma 233 and 6 sigma 3.4 (Day 3).
distractor_notes: 2.5 would be the long-term value with the shift removed; the table already includes the shift.
3.0 sigma corresponds to 66 807 DPMO.
5.5 adds the shift twice.

stem: Which of the following best describes what "defining a process" produces in the Define phase?
options: An agreed statement of the process's start and end points, its inputs and suppliers, its outputs and customers, and its owner
A control plan for the process owner
A list of confirmed root causes
A detailed flowchart of every decision and loop
explanation: Defining a process fixes what is being studied: boundaries, inputs, outputs, customers and owner, usually written as a SIPOC. Detailed mapping comes in Measure, causes in Analyse and the control plan in Control (Day 4).
distractor_notes: The control plan is a Control deliverable.
Root causes come from Analyse.
Detailed flowcharts are process mapping, a Measure activity.

subtopic: Basic Six Sigma Metrics (DPU, DPMO, FTY, RTY, Cycle Time)
stem: Using the standard sigma table with the 1.5-sigma shift, how many defects per million opportunities does a 4.5 sigma process produce?
explanation: A 4.5 sigma process on the table is 3.0 sigma on the normal distribution after the 1.5 shift is removed, which gives 1 350 DPMO. 3.4 DPMO is 6 sigma, 6 210 is 4 sigma and 233 is 5 sigma (Day 3).
distractor_notes: 233 is 5 sigma.
3.4 DPMO is the 6 sigma figure; 4.5 sigma without the shift is where 3.4 comes from on the plain normal curve, but the table reports it as 6.
6,210 is 4 sigma.

subtopic: Basic Six Sigma Metrics (DPU, DPMO, FTY, RTY, Cycle Time)
stem: A late-delivery rate fell from 12% to 7% after a trial. By what percentage was the late-delivery rate reduced?
explanation: The reduction is (12 − 7) ÷ 12 × 100 = 41.7%. The 5-percentage-point drop is the absolute change; the percentage reduction is relative to the starting rate (Day 3).
distractor_notes: 5.0% is the change in percentage points, not the percentage reduction.
71.4% divides by the new rate (5 ÷ 7) instead of the old.
58.3% is 7 ÷ 12, the share of the original rate that remains.

subtopic: Building a Business Case & Project Charter
stem: Which of the following must NOT appear in a project charter's problem statement?
options: The measured size of the problem
The impact on the customer or the business
The period over which it was measured
The suspected cause and the proposed solution
explanation: A problem statement says what, where, when, how much and with what impact. Naming a cause or a solution commits the team before any data has been analysed, which is exactly what DMAIC is designed to prevent (Day 4).
distractor_notes: The measured Y is essential: it is the "how much".
Impact is one of the five required elements.
The period is the "when".

subtopic: Building a Business Case & Project Charter
stem: Which of these is the best problem statement for a charter?
options: "We will reduce invoice errors to 3% by November by retraining the data entry team."

"Between January and June, 9% of the 3,000 invoices raised each month at the Perth office contained at least one error, causing an average 21-day payment delay and about $15,400 a month in credit notes and rework."
"Customers are unhappy with our invoices and the team needs to do better."
"Invoicing is inefficient because the pricing system is outdated and must be replaced."
explanation: The second statement has a place, a period, a measured Y (9% of 3 000 a month) and an impact, and it names no cause or solution. The others contain a cause, have no numbers, or are a goal with a solution built in (Day 4).
distractor_notes: This is a goal statement, and it names a solution.
No place, period, number or impact.
This names a cause (outdated system) and a solution (replace it) and has no measurement.

subtopic: Building a Business Case & Project Charter
stem: Which element of the project charter states what the primary metric will be, and by what date?
options: Problem statement
Goal statement
Scope
Business case
explanation: The goal statement commits to a value of the Y by a date, using the same measure as the problem statement, and is tested against SMART. The business case says why the project matters, the problem statement says what is wrong now, and scope says what is in and out (Day 4).
distractor_notes: The problem statement describes the current situation, not the target.
Scope defines boundaries, not targets.
The business case explains why the organisation should fund the project.

subtopic: Building a Business Case & Project Charter
stem: The problem statement of a charter describes an invoice error rate of 9%. Which goal statement is consistent with it and passes the SMART test?
options: "Reduce the invoice error rate from 9% to 3% by 30 November."
"Reduce invoice cycle time from 2.3 days to 1 day by 30 November."
"Improve invoicing accuracy significantly."
"Implement the new pricing module by 30 November."
explanation: The goal uses the same measure as the problem (error rate), gives a number and a date, and describes an outcome rather than a solution. Cycle time is a different measure, and implementing a module is a solution, not a goal (Day 4).
distractor_notes: The measure does not match the problem statement's Y.
"Significantly" is neither specific nor measurable.
A goal must not name the solution, which is unknown in Define.

subtopic: Building a Business Case & Project Charter
stem: Who signs the project charter, and what happens to it after Define?
options: The Green Belt signs it and it is filed until the project ends
The Champion signs it and it is revisited at every tollgate, with any change of goal or scope agreed with the Champion
The process owner signs it and it is replaced by the control plan
The Master Black Belt signs it and rewrites it in each phase
explanation: The charter is the Champion's authorisation of the project and the reference at every tollgate. Numbers may be refined once Measure produces a baseline, but the goal and scope are not changed without the Champion (Day 4).
distractor_notes: The Green Belt drafts the charter; the Champion authorises it, and it is used throughout.
The control plan is a Control deliverable that supplements, not replaces, the charter.
The Master Black Belt coaches; they do not own the charter.

subtopic: Building a Business Case & Project Charter
stem: What is the purpose of the business case in a project charter?
options: To describe the statistical tools that will be used
To list the team members and their time commitment
To state why the organisation should fund this project: what the problem costs, what improvement is worth and what happens if nothing is done
To record the customer's requirements in their own words
explanation: The business case is the voice of the business written down: the argument the Champion uses to defend the project. It uses cost of poor quality thinking and its numbers must be checkable (Day 4).
distractor_notes: Tools are chosen as the project proceeds; they are not in the business case.
Team membership is the team element of the charter.
Customer requirements are captured in the voice of the customer and the CTQ tree.

stem: How many primary metrics should a Lean Six Sigma project have?
options: At least three, to cover cost, quality and time
As many as the Champion requests
One for each team member
One, the measure of the Y used in the problem and goal statements
explanation: A project has one primary metric: the Y that is baselined in Measure and tracked through Control, written in the same units as the goal statement. Other measures are secondary metrics (Day 5).
distractor_notes: Cost, quality and time may all be watched, but only one is the primary metric; the others are secondary.
The Champion may want many measures, but the project is defined by one primary metric.
Metrics belong to the project, not to individuals.

stem: A project cut invoice errors from 9% to 2%, but the finance director complains that invoices now take four days instead of two to issue because everything is double-checked. What should the project have tracked to catch this earlier?
options: The sigma level of the double-check
A consequential (guard-rail) metric for invoice lead time
The voice of the employee
A second primary metric
explanation: Consequential metrics protect against fixing one thing by breaking another. Lead time (order receipt to invoice issue) was the obvious side effect of adding checks, so it should have been a consequential metric with a baseline from the start. Secondary metrics are the x's expected to move; they would not have caught this (Day 5).
distractor_notes: The check's sigma level would not reveal the delay it causes.
The voice of the employee is about the workers' experience, not about the process side effect.
A project has one primary metric; side effects are watched with consequential metrics.

stem: What is a baseline?
options: The target value in the goal statement
The value of a metric before the improvement, measured over enough time to capture normal variation
The lowest value the metric has ever reached
The specification limit set by the customer
explanation: The baseline is where the metric stands now, usually from three to twelve months of historical data so that normal variation is included. The gap between baseline and target is the project's benefit (Day 5).
distractor_notes: The target is the goal; the baseline is the starting point.
A single best value is not representative of normal performance.
Specification limits come from the customer and describe acceptability, not current performance.

stem: A project has one-off costs of $48,000 and is expected to save $6,500 a month. What is the payback period?
options: 0.14 months
78.0 months
13.5 months
7.4 months
explanation: Payback period is one-off cost divided by the saving per period: 48 000 ÷ 6 500 = 7.4 months. The answer takes the units of the saving period (Day 5).
distractor_notes: 0.14 is the saving divided by the cost, the wrong way round.
78.0 treats the monthly saving as an annual figure and multiplies instead of dividing.
13.5 months divides by the saving as if it were $3 550, or confuses payback with 1 ÷ ROI.

stem: A project delivers $78,000 of hard benefit in its first year and cost $48,000. What is the first-year return on investment?
explanation: Return on investment is (benefit − cost) ÷ cost × 100 = (78 000 − 48 000) ÷ 48 000 × 100 = 62.5% (Day 5).
distractor_notes: 30.0% is the net benefit in thousands read as a percentage.
38.5% divides the net benefit by the benefit instead of the cost.
162.5% is benefit ÷ cost, without subtracting the cost.

stem: Which of the following is a hard benefit?
options: Two hours a week of a supervisor's time freed up, which they now spend on other duties
The risk of a regulatory penalty is lower
Staff morale improves because there is less rework
A monthly $4,000 reduction in credit notes issued to customers
explanation: A hard benefit appears in the profit and loss account and can be audited. Fewer credit notes is money not paid out. Morale, lower risk and freed time that is not removed from the payroll are soft benefits (Day 5).
distractor_notes: Freed time is soft unless the position or paid hours are actually removed.
Lower risk is a soft benefit; only an avoided budgeted cost would count as hard in some organisations.
Morale is real but not money in the accounts.

stem: Who validates the savings claimed by a Lean Six Sigma project, and on what basis?
options: The Green Belt, using the estimate in the charter
The Champion, using the goal statement
The financial representative, using measured results after the improvement is implemented, net of costs
The Master Black Belt, using the sigma level
explanation: Benefits capture requires a member of the finance team to agree the calculation method in Define and to sign off the realised saving, measured against the baseline for an agreed period (usually twelve months) after handover, with project costs subtracted (Day 5).
distractor_notes: The belt calculates but does not validate; the charter figure is a forecast.
The Champion sponsors the project but does not audit its financial result.
Sigma level is a defect measure, not a financial validation.

stem: A project will reduce defective invoices by 180 a month. Each defective invoice costs $18 to rework and, for 60% of them, a further $65 credit note, giving an average cost of $57 per defective invoice. What is the annual hard saving?
explanation: Monthly saving = 180 × $57 = $10 260. Annual saving = $10 260 × 12 = $123 120. The cost per defective was given already averaged; it is not recomputed (Day 5).
distractor_notes: $38,880 uses only the $18 rework cost (180 × 18 × 12).
$10,260 is the monthly saving, not the annual figure.
$179,280 uses $18 + $65 = $83 per invoice, ignoring that only 60% incur the credit note.

subtopic: Building a Business Case & Project Charter
stem: A manager proposes a Green Belt project to "install the new scheduling software, which we already know will fix the roster clashes". Why is this a poor candidate for a Lean Six Sigma project?
options: Because roster clashes are not measurable
Because a project cannot start until the software vendor has been selected
Because software projects cannot use DMAIC
Because the solution is already decided, so there is nothing for Measure and Analyse to find; it is a task, not an improvement project
explanation: Project selection favours problems with a clear Y, available data and causes that are not yet known. A problem with a known solution should be handled as an implementation task; forcing it through DMAIC wastes the method (Day 5).
distractor_notes: Roster clashes per week is a perfectly measurable Y.
Vendor selection is part of implementing the known solution; it is not what disqualifies the candidate.
DMAIC applies to any process, including software-supported ones.

stem: Finance reports that a proposed project has a net present value of +$41,000 at the company's 10% discount rate. What does this tell the Green Belt?
options: The project's return on investment is 41%
The project will save exactly $41,000 in its first year
After discounting future savings for the time value of money and subtracting the up-front cost, the project earns more than the company's required 10% rate
The project's payback period is 4.1 years
explanation: Net present value adds the discounted future cash flows and subtracts the initial cost. A positive value means the project beats the discount rate. It is not the first-year saving, the payback period or the ROI (Day 5).
distractor_notes: ROI is (benefit − cost) ÷ cost, a percentage, not a discounted dollar figure.
NPV sums discounted flows over the whole evaluation period; it is not a single year's saving.
Payback period is cost ÷ saving per period, a different calculation.

stem: A project's primary metric is the percentage of invoices with errors. The team also tracks the percentage of orders that arrive with a valid purchase order number, because it expects that to be a cause of errors. What kind of metric is the second one?
options: A consequential metric: a guard-rail against side effects
A secondary metric: a process x expected to move and to explain the primary metric
A primary metric
A financial metric
explanation: Secondary metrics are the process measures (x's) the team expects to change and which explain why the Y moved. Consequential metrics guard against unintended harm to other outputs; this one is a suspected cause, so it is secondary (Day 5).
distractor_notes: A guard-rail metric would be a different output that might worsen, such as cycle time.
There is one primary metric, the Y.
It is a process measure, not a dollar figure.

subtopic: Voice of the Customer, Business and Employee
stem: Which of the following is a proactive source of the voice of the customer?
options: Product returns
Warranty claims
Structured customer interviews
Complaint letters
explanation: Proactive sources are collected on purpose: interviews, surveys, focus groups and observation. Complaints, claims and returns arrive without being asked and are reactive; they under-count problems because most unhappy customers do not speak up (Day 4).
distractor_notes: Returns are reactive.
Warranty claims arrive unprompted: reactive.
Complaints are reactive.

subtopic: Voice of the Customer, Business and Employee
stem: The payroll team complains that 15% of timesheets from the workshop arrive with missing cost codes and have to be sent back. In Six Sigma terms, what is the payroll team?
options: A supplier to the timesheet process
The process owner of the workshop
The voice of the business
The internal customer of the timesheet process, whose requirements define what a defective timesheet is
explanation: Payroll receives the output of the timesheet process, so it is that process's internal customer. Its requirement (a valid cost code) defines the defect, exactly as an external customer's requirement would (Day 4).
distractor_notes: Suppliers provide inputs; payroll receives the output.
The process owner is the manager accountable for the process, not the department that receives its output.
The voice of the business is about cost and strategy, not about who receives the timesheets.
